title: Antim Panghal Confident as India Targets Wrestling Gold at Asian Games
excerpt: The women's 53kg wrestler says a senior-junior mix, three months of joint training and a Japanese coach have the squad ready for Aichi-Nagoya.
body:
• Wrestler Antim Panghal says India's wrestling contingent is confident ahead of the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, pointing to a strong mix of senior and junior wrestlers and three months of joint training.
  • Speaking to ANI, Antim said the team feels no pressure despite medal expectations: "Everyone wants to win a medal, and everyone is preparing to win gold."
  • India won three wrestling bronze medals at Hangzhou and a record 107 medals overall; the 2026 Games run September 19 to October 4.
  • Antim, who competes in the women's 53kg category, is one of six Indian women wrestlers heading to Japan, training under Japanese coach Kosei Akaishi.

Indian wrestler Antim Panghal is confident about India's wrestling contingent ahead of the Asian Games, saying the team has a good mix of senior and junior wrestlers and has been training together for the past three months.

Speaking to ANI on Wednesday, Antim said the wrestlers have been helping and guiding each other during preparations, with the senior members pointing out areas that need improvement. "This time, our team is very good. We have both senior and junior wrestlers," she said.

No pressure, only gold

Despite the weight of expectations on wrestling — traditionally one of India's strongest disciplines at the continental level — Antim insisted the camp is relaxed and focused.

"Everyone wants to win a medal, and everyone is preparing to win gold. We are trying to give our 100 per cent. There is no pressure. We know what we have to fight for, and we train for that."

— Antim Panghal, wrestler

"The Asian Games are important because they are held once every four years, but we will give our 100 per cent," she added. In a separate interview with IANS earlier in the week, Antim elaborated on the camp's mindset: "Our camp is going well. We are all training together with the same mindset of getting a medal for our country. It feels good to be one of the six girls going."

Technique, repetition and a Japanese coach

Antim said the technical side of preparation has been the priority, with the squad drilling its mat work relentlessly rather than chasing separate conditioning programmes.

"We will focus more on our work on the mat. We are focusing on our mistakes and working on them again and again so that we can execute them properly during the bout."

— Antim Panghal, wrestler

The camp has also benefited from the presence of Japanese coach Kosei Akaishi, the discipline's head coach at the Inspire Institute of Sport. "We also have coach Akaishi from Japan who has been helping and teaching us a lot. The Indian team camps are very useful because we all learn a lot from each other," Antim told IANS. She added that competing regularly has hardened her mindset: "When you step into a bout at the Asian Games, you don't feel the immense pressure of the occasion. It feels much like a regular match or even a training session."

The squad

India's 16-member wrestling team spans all three disciplines. The women's freestyle squad: Dipanshi (50kg), Antim Panghal (53kg), Manisha Bhanwala (57kg), Mansi Ahlawat (62kg), Nisha Dahiya (68kg) and Priya Malik (76kg). Men's freestyle: Aman Sehrawat (57kg), Sujeet Kalkal (65kg), Sagar Jaglan (74kg), Deepak Punia (97kg) and Rajat Ruhal (125kg). Greco-Roman: Sumit Dalal (60kg), Deepak (67kg), Aman (77kg), Sunil Kumar (87kg) and Nitesh Kumar (97kg).

Fellow women's team member Manisha Bhanwala echoed Antim's confidence, telling ANI the Asian Championships had given the squad valuable experience at the continental level and that she aims to extend her medal-winning streak dating back to 2022.

The Hangzhou benchmark

India's wrestlers will look to improve on Hangzhou, where the country won three bronze medals in wrestling. Overall, India clinched a record 107 medals at Hangzhou 2022 — 28 gold, 38 silver and 41 bronze — and will look to better that tally in Aichi-Nagoya, where the Games run from September 19 to October 4.

For Antim, the journey has a personal arc: she took up wrestling after her elder sister, a kabaddi player, introduced her to the sport, and went on to become the first Indian to win the Junior World Championship title — without even realising at the time what she had achieved. Now, with a quadrennial Games on the horizon, she says the goal is simple: "When it comes to medals, everyone competes with the same mindset — to win a medal, and ultimately to win gold."
image_caption: Two wrestlers grapple on the mat during a bout. Antim Panghal heads into the Asian Games as one of India’s leading medal hopes in wrestling.
nri_angle: The Asian Games are a marquee quadrennial event for the diaspora's sporting calendar, and wrestling remains one of the disciplines where Indian fans abroad expect podium finishes.
